definition: A DNS record mapping a name to an IPv4 address.
A DNS record mapping a name to an IPv6 address.
Attribute-based access control (NIST SP 800-162): access is decided by policies over attributes of the subject, the resource and the environment.
The average probability that a draft token is accepted in speculative decoding, equal to the sum over tokens of min(p, q). It sets how many tokens each target pass yields.
A short-lived credential issued by an authorization server that a client presents to an API. It may be an opaque reference or a self-contained JWT.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability: the guarantees of a database transaction.
An acknowledgement: a TCP packet field telling the sender which bytes have arrived.

A hidden dimension whose activation values are far larger than the rest, which appears in large transformers. Outliers make naive 8-bit activation quantization lose precision, which methods such as LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant work around.
A redundancy setup where all nodes serve traffic at once and share the load.
A redundancy setup where one node serves traffic and a standby takes over only if it fails.
A cap on in-flight requests that adjusts itself from observed latency, raising the limit while latency is stable and cutting it when latency rises, much like TCP congestion control.
Client-side load shedding in which each client rejects a growing share of its own requests as the backend's acceptance rate falls, as described in Google's SRE book.
The decision at a service's entry point whether to accept a new request, based on the server's own state such as in-flight count, queue wait or utilisation.
The repeated cycle of calling the model, running any tools it requests, appending the results to the history and calling it again until it gives a final answer.
A system in which an LLM dynamically decides which tools to call and in what order until a task is done, instead of following predefined code paths.
The loss of attention that comes from receiving too many false or unactionable alerts, which leads responders to ignore or miss real ones.
An alert repeatedly firing and resolving because its signal hovers around the threshold, sending a notification each time.
Merging related alerts, such as the same alert from many hosts in one cluster, into a single notification. Prometheus Alertmanager does this with group_by labels.
Muting some alerts while another, usually their cause, is firing, so responders see the root problem instead of every downstream effect.

A collective operation in which every rank contributes a tensor and every rank ends up with their element-wise sum. It is equivalent to a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather; a ring all-reduce sends about 2(N − 1)/N times the tensor size per rank.
How long a stream processor keeps a window's state after the watermark passes it, so late events can still update and re-emit the result. Kafka Streams calls this the grace period.
A DDoS technique that sends small spoofed UDP requests to open servers (DNS, NTP, memcached) so their much larger replies flood the victim whose address was forged.
A background process that compares replicas and copies over missing or outdated data, whether or not anyone reads it.
Announcing the same IP address from many locations so the network routes each user to the nearest one.
Shorthand for a system that keeps answering on every side of a network partition and reconciles diverging data afterwards.
A reverse proxy at the edge that routes API requests to back-end services and handles shared concerns like auth and rate limits.
A Redis persistence log of every write command, replayed on restart. Its fsync policy sets how much data a crash can lose.
Vector search that uses an index to examine a small fraction of the vectors and returns results that are usually, but not always, the true nearest neighbours.
The number of floating-point operations a computation performs per byte it moves to or from memory. Compared with a chip's ridge point, it shows whether compute or memory bandwidth limits speed.
Moving the exact build artifact that passed testing (identified by an immutable digest) from environment to environment, changing only configuration and never rebuilding.
A delivery guarantee where each message arrives one or more times, so duplicates are possible.
A delivery guarantee where each message is processed zero or one times: never duplicated, but possibly lost.
Establishing who a caller is, for example by password plus MFA, a certificate or a signed token. Often shortened to authn.
The server that holds a domain's actual records and gives the final answer.
Deciding what an authenticated caller is allowed to do with a given resource. Often shortened to authz.
An integer primary key assigned by the database from a counter or sequence on each insert. Small and ordered on one node, but tied to one counter and gapped by rollbacks.
Automatically adding or removing instances based on a metric such as CPU, request rate or queue depth.
The fraction of time a service works correctly, often written in nines (99.9% is three nines).
One or more data centres in a cloud region with independent power and networking, close enough to other zones for low-latency links but far enough to fail independently.
A balanced tree of fixed-size pages, the default database index, efficient for lookups and range scans.
Quick arithmetic with round numbers to get an answer within a small factor, used to size a design before building it.
A pattern where each client type gets its own thin server-side back end that shapes data for it.
Rerunning a data pipeline for past dates, for example after a bug fix or a new column, which is only safe if each run is idempotent.
A signal from a slow receiver that makes the sender slow down, instead of letting unprocessed work pile up until something fails.
Link bandwidth × round-trip time: how much data must be in flight, unacknowledged, to keep a link fully busy.

The property that a kernel returns bit-identical results for one input whatever else is in the batch. Kernels without it change their reduction order with batch size, which makes temperature-0 output vary with server load.
A token that grants access to whoever presents it, usually sent as Authorization: Bearer. Anyone who copies it can use it.
A model that embeds queries and documents separately into vectors, so document vectors can be precomputed and indexed. Standard embedding models are bi-encoders.
In RabbitMQ, a rule connecting an exchange to a queue, with a key or pattern that decides which messages the queue receives.
How much of a system and its users a failure or experiment can affect, limited by traffic share, scope and duration.
Storage presented as a raw disk of numbered blocks, mounted by one machine.
A compact probabilistic structure that can say an item is definitely not in a set, or possibly in it.
Running two full production environments, deploying to the idle one and switching all traffic to it at once, keeping the old one running for instant rollback.
A ranking function refining TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalisation.
The area of RAM where a database keeps recently used data pages, such as shared_buffers in PostgreSQL or the InnoDB buffer pool in MySQL.
A resilience pattern that splits a limited resource such as threads, connections or servers into separate pools, so exhausting one pool cannot exhaust the others.
How fast the error budget is being spent relative to the pace that would use exactly all of it over the SLO window: observed error rate divided by (1 minus the SLO).
A smaller, faster store that keeps copies of data whose real home is slower or more expensive to reach, so repeated reads can skip the slow path.
A large share of the cache becoming unavailable at once, through synchronised expiry or an empty restart, so the full read load hits the database.
The fraction of cache lookups that find the value in the cache. It sets both average latency and how much load reaches the backing store.
Removing or replacing a cached copy when the data in the source of truth changes.
The identifier a cache stores a response under, such as host, path and query string. Requests with the same key share one cached copy.
A token a cache hands out on a miss and requires on the following set. A delete in between invalidates it, so stale values can't be written back.
A stream of requests for keys that exist in neither the cache nor the database, so every request misses and reaches the database.
Entries that are used once and never again, such as those from scans or batch jobs, pushing reusable entries out of a cache.
Removing or invalidating cached content before its TTL ends, for example by URL, prefix or tag.
When a popular cached value expires or is evicted and many concurrent requests miss at once, all rebuilding it from the database. Also called a dog-pile or thundering herd.
Pre-loading frequently used keys into a cache before it serves traffic, so a cold cache doesn't send a burst of misses to the database.
A caching strategy where the application checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result, and deletes the cached key when it writes. Also called lazy loading or look-aside.
The HTTP header that tells browsers and caches whether, and for how long, a response may be stored and reused.
An automated statistical comparison of a canary's metrics against a baseline of the old version, used to decide whether to promote or abort a release.
Sending a small share of real traffic to a new version, comparing its health with the old version, and widening exposure in steps or aborting.

The result (Brewer's conjecture, proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002) that when a network partition occurs, a replicated system cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and a response from every non-failing node.
A sudden large rise in the number of time series, usually caused by a metric label with unbounded values such as user IDs, which can exhaust a metrics database's memory.
A consistency model in which operations that are causally related are seen by every node in the same order, while concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
A network of servers in many locations that caches content close to users and serves it on behalf of an origin.
A signed document binding a domain name to a public key, issued by a certificate authority.
An organisation trusted by browsers and operating systems to sign certificates after checking who controls a domain.
The sequence from a site's certificate through intermediates up to a trusted root, each signed by the next.

A control group: a Linux kernel feature that accounts for and limits the CPU, memory, I/O and process count of a group of processes. Memory over the limit triggers an OOM kill; CPU over the limit is throttled.
Streaming every insert, update and delete from a database's log into other systems.
The discipline of running controlled experiments on a system, usually in production, to build confidence that it withstands real-world failures.

A consistent snapshot of every operator's state together with the source offsets that produced it; Flink takes one by sending barrier markers through the data streams and restores from it after a failure.
Repeating the end of one chunk at the start of the next so sentences near a boundary appear whole in at least one chunk.
Splitting a long prompt's prefill into fixed-size chunks that share each scheduler iteration with ongoing decode steps, so a long prompt does not freeze every other stream (Sarathi-Serve).
Splitting documents into passages small enough to embed and to fit several into a prompt, by fixed size, by sentences or paragraphs, or by document structure.
The named set of algorithms a TLS connection uses for key exchange, encryption and integrity.
A wrapper around calls to a dependency that stops calling it when its failure rate crosses a threshold, failing fast for a while and then testing recovery with a few trial calls.
Requiring every claim in a generated answer to point to a source passage that was in the context, and verifying those citations before showing the answer.
A program that starts a request: a browser, a mobile app, another service or a scheduled job.
The rate at which a clock gains or loses time relative to true time, often given in parts per million. Drift is why clocks need regular synchronisation.
The difference between two clocks' readings at the same instant. Skew between servers makes timestamps from different machines unreliable for ordering events.
A DNS record that makes one name an alias for another name.
An invocation that must wait for a new execution environment to be created and initialised before the handler runs, adding latency compared with reusing a warm one.
Storing each column's values together on disk, so queries read only the columns they need.
A reduce-like function run on each map task's output before the shuffle to pre-aggregate it; valid only for mergeable operations such as sum, count, min and max.
A message asking one specific handler to do something, named in the imperative (ReserveStock); the handler may reject it.
The highest Raft log position known to be stored on a majority. Entries at or below it are permanent and appear in every future leader's log.
An append-only, ordered sequence of records on disk where each record has a position number; a Kafka partition is a commit log.
An atomic write that succeeds only if the current value or version still matches what the writer expects, giving mutual exclusion on one record without a lock.
A forward action that semantically undoes an earlier saga step, such as a refund for a charge or a release for a reservation. The original effect stays in history.
A pattern where several identical workers read from one queue and each message is handled by just one of them, spreading the work.
An index on several columns, sorted by the first, then the second, and so on.
Splitting a fixed compute budget between model size and training tokens to minimise loss. The Chinchilla paper found roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
A request with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since that returns 304 Not Modified, with no body, if the cached copy is still current.
Any difference between what infrastructure code declares and what is actually running, usually caused by changes made outside the tool.
A privileged program tricked into using its authority on behalf of a caller who lacks that authority. Fixed by checking the original caller's rights, not just the intermediary's.
Algorithms (slow start, CUBIC, BBR) that limit how fast TCP sends so it does not overload the network between hosts.
A set of open database connections that an application reuses instead of opening one per request.
An HTTP request with an Upgrade header asking the server to switch the connection to another protocol, such as WebSocket.
The problem of getting several machines to agree on one value or sequence of values, so that once decided it never changes and every node learns the same decision, despite crashes and lost messages.
A contract between a data store and its clients that defines which values a read may return given the history of writes.
Mapping keys and servers onto a ring so adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys.
Restricting which tokens a model may generate at each step so the output must match a grammar or schema. It guarantees syntax, not correct values.
A set of consumers sharing a group ID that split a topic's partitions so each partition is read by exactly one member; separate groups each read every message.
How far a consumer group is behind the newest data: log-end offset minus committed offset per partition, or the age of the oldest unprocessed message.
In a log-based broker such as Kafka, the position of the next message a consumer group will read in a partition. Committing it records progress.

A normal host process started with Linux namespaces that limit what it can see and cgroups that limit what it can use, running from an image's filesystem. It shares the host kernel, unlike a virtual machine.
A read-only template for a container: an ordered list of filesystem layers plus metadata such as the default command, environment and user, defined by the OCI image specification.
A server that stores and distributes container images by repository, tag and digest, such as Docker Hub, Amazon ECR or a self-hosted registry.

The software that creates and runs containers on a host. High-level runtimes such as containerd and CRI-O manage images and lifecycle; low-level runtimes such as runc set up namespaces and cgroups and start the process.

Splitting one long sequence across GPUs for every operation, including attention, for example by passing key/value blocks round a ring (Ring Attention). Used when activations for long contexts do not fit.
Passing the trace ID and current span ID from one service to the next, usually in the W3C traceparent header, so spans join one trace.
Iteration-level scheduling for LLM inference, introduced by Orca: batch membership is decided at every decode step, so finished sequences leave immediately and waiting requests join.
Keeping every change that passes the pipeline releasable, so production deployment is a single action whose timing a person or schedule chooses.
Automatically deploying every change that passes the pipeline to production, with no human gate.
The practice of merging small changes into the shared mainline at least daily, with every merge automatically built and tested.
The part of a system that changes it, such as launching instances, scaling groups and updating routes or configuration.
The observation that systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them.
An operating-system technique where a forked process shares memory pages with its parent and a page is copied only when one side modifies it.
A single cause, such as a bad deploy, a poison request or a zone outage, taking out many supposedly redundant copies at the same time.
A unique ID assigned when a request enters a system and carried to every service, message and job it causes, so all their log lines can be joined. Often called a request ID.
The dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths, measuring the angle between them from −1 to 1. For unit-length vectors it equals the dot product.
A metric whose value only increases, resetting to zero when the process restarts. You query its rate of increase, not its raw value.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself is not read.
Shorthand for a system that, during a network partition, refuses some requests rather than risk returning inconsistent data.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: using separate models for writes and for reads, with read models updated from the write side, usually asynchronously.
A conflict-free replicated data type: a data structure, such as a counter, set or text sequence, designed so concurrent updates on different replicas always merge to the same result.
The chain of operations in a request that determined its total latency; speeding up anything off this chain does not make the request faster.
A sequence of steps a user cares about completing, such as search, add to cart and pay. SLIs are chosen to measure whether these journeys work.
A model that reads a query and one candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score. More accurate than a bi-encoder but too slow to run over a whole corpus, so it is used for reranking.
Sending traffic that a region cannot serve to another region with spare capacity, accepting extra network latency and subject to data-residency rules.
Injection into a web page: untrusted data inserted into HTML or JavaScript without encoding runs as script in other users' browsers with their session.
Deleting data by destroying the key it was encrypted with, so every copy, including immutable backups, becomes permanently unreadable.
A recorded sequence of GPU kernel launches that can be replayed with a single call, removing per-kernel CPU launch overhead. It requires fixed tensor shapes.
Running new code on real production traffic without showing users its results, to test capacity and correctness before release.
A symmetric key that encrypts the actual data. It is stored only in wrapped form next to the ciphertext and unwrapped by the KMS when needed.
Raw data files of any kind kept cheaply in object storage for many engines to query.
How close the data a computation needs is to where the computation runs. Poor locality turns every data access into a long network round trip.
Training with a full copy of the model on every GPU, each processing a different slice of the batch, with gradients all-reduced each step so the copies stay identical.
The part of a system that serves each request, such as running instances, load balancers forwarding traffic and databases answering queries.
A requirement, from law, regulation or contract, that certain data be stored and processed within a particular geography.
An uneven distribution in which a few keys hold a large share of the records, so the tasks handling them take far longer than the rest.
The principle that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is physically located, which can differ from the laws of the user's or company's home country.
A system storing cleaned, structured data for analytical SQL queries.
A self-contained packet sent without a connection; UDP's unit of data.
A utility that batches many single-key lookups made at the same time into one query and caches them per request.
Daily active users: the number of distinct users who use the product on a given day.
A distributed denial-of-service attack: traffic from many sources at once exhausts bandwidth, connection state or server capacity so legitimate users can't be served.
An alert that is always firing on purpose and is expected by an external service, which pages if it stops arriving because the alerting pipeline has broken.
A separate queue that receives messages after they have failed too many times, so the main queue keeps flowing and the failures can be inspected.
An absolute time by which a caller gives up on a call; propagated to downstream calls in gRPC.
Passing a request's absolute deadline, or its remaining time, to every downstream call so each hop uses only what is left and stops when it expires. gRPC does this with the grpc-timeout header.
A state where transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so none can proceed.
Describing the desired end state of infrastructure and letting a tool compute and apply the changes needed to reach it, so repeated runs change nothing.
The phase of LLM inference that generates output one token per step per sequence. Each step reads all model weights, so it is limited by memory bandwidth.
A ranked list of progressively simpler ways to serve a feature, from the primary model down to a non-AI path or a clear 'unavailable' message, decided in advance.
Deleting a cache key after a database update and again after a short delay, to remove any stale value a slow concurrent reader wrote back.
A replica that deliberately applies changes a fixed time behind the primary, so a recent mistake can be stopped before it reaches the replica.
Deliberately storing data in more than one place to make reads cheaper.
A Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of identical pods running and rolls out new versions by gradually replacing one ReplicaSet with another.
An automated sequence of build, test and deploy stages that each commit passes through, cheapest first; a failure at any stage stops the change.
A method for two parties to agree on a shared secret over a public channel without an eavesdropper being able to compute it.
A separate cluster of in-memory key-value servers, such as Redis or Memcached, shared by all application servers over the network.
Services that must be deployed together or share a database: the costs of microservices without their independence.
Recording the path and timing of one request through every service it touches, as a tree of spans sharing a trace ID.
The Domain Name System: the distributed directory that turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
A trick where a hostname resolves to a safe public address when it is checked and to an internal address when it is actually fetched, defeating validation that resolves twice.
A database that stores self-contained, nested JSON-like documents.
The small, fast model in speculative decoding that proposes candidate tokens for the target model to verify. It must share the target's vocabulary.
Updating two separate systems, such as a database and a message broker, without a shared transaction, so a failure between the writes leaves them inconsistent.
A credential generated on demand for one requester with a lease, and revoked automatically when the lease expires, such as a temporary database user created by Vault.
Running application code in many locations close to users, typically a CDN's points of presence, instead of only in a few central regions.
Code that runs inside a CDN's points of presence on the request path, able to inspect, rewrite, answer or forward requests before they reach the cache or origin.
A markup language, published as a W3C Note in 2001, that lets a CDN assemble a page at the edge from separately cached fragments.

A DNS extension (RFC 7871) that lets a recursive resolver pass a truncated version of the client's IP subnet to the authoritative server, so location-based answers reflect the user rather than the resolver.
At-least-once delivery combined with idempotent consumers or broker transactions, so duplicates may arrive but each message's effect is applied once.
Data leaving a system or network, such as responses and downloads. Cloud providers usually charge for it.
A distributed search engine built on Apache Lucene that splits indexes into replicated shards.
How long a Raft follower waits without hearing from a leader before becoming a candidate. It is randomised (the Raft paper's example is 150 to 300 ms) so split votes are rare.
Extract, load, transform: landing raw data in a warehouse or lake first and transforming it there, usually with SQL, so the raw data stays available for reprocessing.
A fixed-length vector of numbers produced by a model so that inputs with similar meaning get nearby vectors. Vectors from different models are not comparable.
Encrypting data locally with a data encryption key, then encrypting (wrapping) that key with a key-encryption key held in a KMS and storing the wrapped key beside the ciphertext.
An open-source L7 proxy built for service-to-service traffic, commonly used as a sidecar in service meshes.
A ZooKeeper znode that is deleted automatically when the client session that created it ends. Lock and leader-election recipes rely on it.
The amount of unreliability an SLO allows over its window, equal to 1 minus the SLO. A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows 0.1% bad requests, or 43.2 minutes of full outage.
A document agreed in advance by engineering, product and leadership that says what changes, such as a release freeze, when a service spends its error budget.
A version tag a server attaches to a response so a client can later ask 'has this changed?' cheaply.
Extract, transform, load: pulling data from sources, cleaning and reshaping it in a separate processing step, then loading the finished tables into an analytical store.
A message stating that something has already happened, named in the past tense (OrderPlaced), published for any number of subscribers to react to.
A single thread that waits for ready I/O events and handles them one at a time, as Redis does for command execution.
Storing the full sequence of events as the source of truth and deriving current state by replaying them, instead of storing only current state.
The time an event actually happened, stamped by the device or service that produced it.
An event style where the event includes the changed data, so consumers can keep their own copy instead of calling the source service back.
A guarantee that if no new updates are made to an object, all replicas eventually return the same last value. It promises nothing about timing or what reads return meanwhile.
The rule a full cache uses to choose which entry to remove to make room for a new one, such as LRU or LFU.
The promise that each message's effect happens exactly once. True exactly-once delivery is impossible across crashes; real systems offer effectively-once processing.
In RabbitMQ, the component producers publish to; it routes each message to queues according to its type (direct, topic, fanout or headers) and its bindings.

The isolated sandbox a function platform creates to run your code, holding the runtime, your code and scratch storage. In AWS Lambda it goes through Init, Invoke and Shutdown phases and handles one invocation at a time.
A trace ID attached to a metric sample, such as a histogram bucket, so a point on a graph links to a real request's trace.
A pattern for incompatible changes (also called parallel change): expand the schema or interface to support old and new, migrate, then contract by removing the old shape once nothing uses it.
Placing the experts of a mixture-of-experts layer on different GPUs and moving each token to its chosen expert and back with two all-to-all exchanges per layer.
A retry strategy that multiplies the wait after each failure (usually doubling it) up to a cap, so a struggling service gets progressively more time to recover.
Treating an unavailable check as if it failed and rejecting the request. Suits checks like authentication where a wrong yes causes harm.
Rejecting a request immediately when it is known it cannot succeed, instead of waiting for a timeout, so resources are freed and the caller can react at once.
Treating an unavailable check as if it passed and letting the request through. Suits checks like rate limiters where a wrong yes is cheap.
Returning service to the original site after a failover, which requires copying back the writes made during the failover and is itself a second failover.
Shifting work from a failed component to a redundant one, for example promoting a standby database and redirecting clients to it.

Scheduling that serves competing clients in proportion to assigned weights instead of arrival order, so one client's burst cannot starve the others. For LLMs it is usually measured in tokens served, not requests.
The planned alternative response when a dependency is unavailable, such as a cached value, a default, a degraded page, deferred work or a clear error.
One request triggering many parallel sub-requests, often waiting for all of them to answer.
The effect where rare slow responses on each backend become common for requests that wait on many backends.
Deliberately introducing a failure, such as killing a process, adding latency or returning errors, to observe how a system responds.
The ability of a system to keep providing its service, possibly in a reduced form, while some of its components have failed.
A runtime switch in code that turns behaviour on or off for chosen users without a deploy, separating deploying code from releasing it.
A number that increases with every lock grant and is sent with each write. The protected resource rejects writes carrying a lower token than one it has already accepted.
A test that passes and fails on the same code, usually from timing, ordering or shared state; small flake rates compound across a large suite.
An exact, IO-aware attention kernel (Dao et al., 2022) that tiles queries, keys and values into on-chip SRAM and uses an online softmax, so the N × N score matrix is never written to GPU memory.
Preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver; in TCP the receiver advertises how much buffer space it has.
A column that refers to the primary key of another table, which the database can enforce.
One run of a model from input token IDs through every layer to a score for each possible next token. Generating one token takes one forward pass.
A server in front of clients that sends their requests out to the internet on their behalf.
A property where per-session keys mean a long-term private key stolen later cannot decrypt previously recorded traffic.

An 8-bit floating-point number format (commonly the E4M3 and E5M2 variants) used for weights, activations or the KV cache. Its exponent gives it a wider range than INT8, and recent datacenter GPUs run matrix maths on it natively.
A retry delay drawn uniformly between zero and the capped exponential backoff: sleep = random_between(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)).
Both sides can send at the same time, independently.
A compute model where you deploy individual handler functions and the platform runs, scales and bills them per invocation, with no servers for you to manage.
A grow-only counter CRDT: each replica increments only its own slot, merging takes the per-slot maximum, and the value is the sum of all slots.
A scheduled exercise in which a team triggers a failure scenario and practises responding, testing people, runbooks and paging as well as software.
Allocating and running all of a job's processes together or not at all. Synchronous training jobs need it, so one lost GPU stops the whole job.
A metric whose value can go up and down, such as memory in use or queue depth, read as a current level.
The billing unit for function compute: configured memory in gigabytes multiplied by billed run time in seconds. 512 MB for 100 ms is 0.05 GB-seconds.
DNS that returns different answers depending on where the resolver appears to be, steering users to a nearby region.
The rate of successful responses delivered within the client's deadline. Under overload, throughput can stay high while goodput falls towards zero.
Keeping a system's core function working with reduced quality when an optional dependency fails, instead of failing the whole request.
A database that stores nodes and edges directly and traverses relationships without joins.
A query language and runtime for APIs where clients request exactly the fields they need from a typed schema.
Always choosing the single most likely next token (the argmax of the logits). Most APIs treat temperature 0 as greedy decoding.
An attention design in which several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache per token. Llama 2 70B uses 8 KV heads for 64 query heads.
A variant of the gRPC protocol that browsers can send, translated to native gRPC by a proxy.
A check that runs outside the prompt, before or after a model call, to block or rewrite unsafe inputs and outputs.
Data flows in only one direction at a time; SSE is effectively one-way, server to client.
The circuit breaker state after the open wait, in which a limited number of trial calls are let through to decide whether to close or reopen.
Lamport's relation a → b: a precedes b in the same process, or a sends a message that b receives, or a chain of these links them. Events not related either way are concurrent.
One of the 16,384 buckets Redis Cluster divides keys into, computed as CRC16(key) mod 16384. Each primary node owns a range of slots.
Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State: API responses include links to the actions available next.
Deciding at the start of a trace whether to record it and passing the decision downstream. Cheap, but it keeps errors only at the sample rate.
When one lost or slow item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it.
A periodic probe a load balancer sends to each backend to decide whether it should receive traffic.
A small periodic message (ping) sent to prove a connection or node is still alive.
Sending a second copy of a slow, idempotent request to another replica after about the p95 latency and using whichever answer arrives first, to cut tail latency.
Designing a system to keep serving while individual components fail, through redundancy plus fast detection and failover.
Storing a write meant for an unreachable replica, together with a hint naming that replica, and forwarding it when the replica comes back.
A metric that counts observations into buckets, plus their sum and count, so percentiles can be estimated and aggregated across instances.
A graph-based ANN index with sparse upper layers for long greedy hops and a dense bottom layer searched with a candidate list of size efSearch. Introduced by Malkov and Yashunin.
The one region where a given user's or entity's data is written in a multi-region system. Other regions may serve reads but forward writes there, which avoids write conflicts.
A Kubernetes controller that sets a workload's replica count to ceil(current replicas × current metric ÷ target), evaluated every 15 seconds by default.
Adding capacity by running more machines or copies of a service, rather than making one machine bigger.
A single cache key receiving so much traffic that it overloads the one node that stores it.
A shard receiving far more traffic than the others, often because of one very popular key.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request–response protocol of the web, with methods, headers, status codes and bodies.
The 2015 revision of HTTP with binary framing, header compression and many concurrent streams over one connection.
A design where an automated system pauses for a person to approve, edit or reject an action before it takes effect.
A timestamp combining wall-clock time with a logical counter, so it stays close to real time, never goes backwards and respects happens-before. Used by CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.
Running keyword search (such as BM25) and vector search for the same query and merging the result lists, so both exact tokens and paraphrases are matched.
A probabilistic structure that estimates the number of distinct items using very little memory. In Redis it uses at most 12 KB with about 0.81% standard error.
A property of an operation where doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, which makes retries safe.
A unique ID a client sends with every retry of one operation so the server performs it only once.
A message consumer that produces the same effect even if it receives the same message more than once.
An HTTP method where repeating the same request has the same effect as sending it once, such as PUT or DELETE.
A producer whose retries can't create duplicates; in Kafka the broker uses a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers to discard repeated sends.
The SHA-256 hash of an image's manifest, which names one exact image forever. Unlike a tag, it cannot be moved to point at different bytes.
A content-addressed tarball of the files one build step added, changed or deleted. Layers are stacked by a union filesystem and shared between images that use them.
A backup that cannot be changed or deleted until its retention period ends, even by an administrator, protecting it from ransomware and runaway scripts.
Replacing servers with freshly built images instead of patching them in place, so no machine accumulates undocumented changes.
A 2PC participant's transaction after it voted YES but before it learned the decision. It can neither commit nor abort on its own and must keep its locks.
A cache that lives in the application's own memory, giving nanosecond lookups but a separate, independently expiring copy on every server.
A separate data structure that stores some columns in sorted or hashed order with pointers to rows, so queries can find them without scanning.
Defining infrastructure such as networks, servers, databases and permissions in version-controlled files that a tool turns into real resources.
A Kubernetes object holding layer 7 host and path routing rules for traffic entering the cluster. An ingress controller must watch it and configure a real proxy.
A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, used by search engines.
A setting that decides which concurrency anomalies a transaction can see.
An ANN index that clusters vectors around k-means centroids into lists and, at query time, scans only the nprobe lists whose centroids are closest to the query.
Randomness added to retry delays so clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry at the same moment.
A signed token that carries claims such as a user id and expiry, so servers can verify it without a lookup. Hard to revoke before it expires.
JSON Web Key Set: a document an issuer publishes at a known URL listing its public signing keys, each with a key ID (kid) that tokens reference.
An ID that is roughly ordered by creation time: sorting by ID gives creation order except for IDs made close together on different machines.
Jay Kreps's alternative to lambda: a single stream processing codebase over a retained, replayable log, reprocessing history by replaying the log into a new output.
Reusing one TCP connection for several HTTP requests instead of opening a new one each time.
A managed service that holds master keys inside hardware security modules, never exports them, and performs encrypt, decrypt and data-key operations under access policies with an audit log.
A key, usually kept inside a KMS or HSM, whose only job is to encrypt and decrypt data encryption keys. Rotating it needs only re-wrapping, not re-encrypting data.
A database that stores opaque values looked up only by their key.

GPU memory holding the attention key and value vectors for every token already processed, so each decode step only computes them for the newest token. Its size is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value, per token.
Balancing on IP addresses and ports at the transport layer, without reading the HTTP request.
Balancing on application data such as the URL path, headers or cookies, which requires parsing HTTP.
A design named by Nathan Marz that runs a batch layer recomputing complete views from immutable data, a speed layer for recent events, and a serving layer that merges them.
A per-process counter incremented on each event and set to max(local, received) + 1 on receive. If a happens before b, a's timestamp is lower, but not the other way round.

A conflict-resolution rule that keeps the write with the highest timestamp and discards the others. It always converges but silently loses concurrent updates, and clock skew can make it keep the earlier write.
How long one operation takes from start to finish, measured in time per request.
A DNS routing policy, such as Amazon Route 53's, that answers each query with the region that has the lowest measured latency from the querying resolver's network.
Replication where one leader accepts all writes and followers copy its log.
Replication where clients write to and read from several replicas directly, using quorums.
A rate-limiting algorithm that queues requests and releases them at a fixed rate.
A lock or right granted for a limited time that the holder must renew. If the holder dies, the lease expires and someone else can take over.
A balancing method that sends each new request to the server with the fewest active connections.
The principle that every user and program should run with only the privileges its job needs, which limits the damage any bug or leaked credential can do.
An eviction policy that removes the entry with the lowest access count, usually with counts that decay over time.
A consistency model in which every operation appears to take effect atomically at one instant between its start and end, in real-time order, as if there were a single copy of the data.
A kernel feature that gives a process its own private copy of one kind of global resource, such as process IDs, network interfaces, mounts or hostname.
L = λW: the average number of items in a stable system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside.
Moving a running request, including its KV cache, from one replica to another while it keeps decoding, then switching over in a short final step (as in Llumnix).
A periodic check that decides whether a container is stuck beyond recovery. On failure the kubelet kills and restarts the container.
Using a language model to grade another model's output against a rubric. It scales grading but has known biases and must be calibrated against human labels.
A component that receives requests and spreads them across several backend servers, skipping servers that fail health checks.
Using a queue to absorb bursts of work so a downstream service processes at a steady rate it can handle.
Deliberately rejecting some requests when a server is overloaded so it can keep serving the rest within their deadlines.
A marker a transaction holds on data to stop other transactions from changing (or locking) it until it finishes.
Collecting logs from every service and machine into one searchable store, also called centralized logging.
A Kafka cleanup policy that keeps at least the latest record for each key and removes older records with the same key.
A severity tag on a log event, such as DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR or FATAL, used to filter and route events by importance.
The policy that deletes old records from a log by age or total size, regardless of whether consumers have read them; Kafka's default is 7 days.
Keeping only a fraction of log events to control cost. It is safest done per request ID rather than per line, while keeping every error.
An agent, such as Fluent Bit, Vector or the OpenTelemetry Collector, that reads logs on a node, adds metadata, buffers them and forwards them to a log store.
A fixed amount added to the logits of chosen token IDs before sampling, used to favour or effectively ban specific tokens.
The raw, unnormalised scores a language model outputs, one per vocabulary token. A softmax (with a temperature) turns them into probabilities.
The client sends a request and the server holds it open until there is data or a timeout, then the client asks again.

A speculative method that needs no draft model: it generates candidate n-grams with parallel Jacobi-style iterations inside the target's own passes and verifies them in the same pass (Fu et al., 2024).
An eviction policy that removes the entry whose last access is oldest.
A write-optimised storage structure that buffers writes in memory and flushes them as sorted immutable files merged by compaction.

A batch programming model from Google (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) where you write a map function that emits key-value pairs and a reduce function that combines all values for a key, and the framework handles distribution and failures.
The Redis setting that decides what happens when the maxmemory limit is reached: reject writes (noeviction, the default) or evict keys by LRU, LFU, random or TTL.
Extra decoding heads added on top of a model's final hidden state, each predicting a token several positions ahead, so the model drafts its own candidates for speculative decoding (Cai et al., 2024).
A tree of hashes in which each leaf hashes a range of data and each parent hashes its children, so two replicas can find differences by comparing only the branches whose hashes differ.
A signal from a consumer telling the broker it has finished processing a message, so the broker can stop redelivering it.
A server that accepts messages from producers, stores them durably and delivers them to consumers, so the two sides don't talk directly.
In SQS FIFO queues, the attribute that defines an ordering group: messages with the same group ID are delivered strictly in order, different groups in parallel.
A point-to-point channel where each message is delivered to exactly one consumer and removed once it has been processed.
A failure that persists after its trigger is removed because a feedback loop, often retries, keeps load above the system's capacity.
A key-value pair, such as route or status, that splits a metric into separate time series you can filter and group by. Called a tag or attribute in some systems.
A separately deployable service that owns one business capability and its data, and talks to other services over the network.
A routing pattern that tries a cheaper model first, checks its output, and escalates to a more capable model only when the check fails.
Observed training throughput in useful model FLOPs divided by the hardware's peak FLOP/s. Unlike hardware FLOPs utilisation, it excludes recomputed work.
Choosing which model handles each request, for example sending easy requests to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a large model.
A single deployable whose modules own their own code and data and only call each other through defined interfaces.
An application built and deployed as one unit. It can still run as many identical copies behind a load balancer.
A clock that only moves forward, such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC or System.nanoTime(). Use it to measure durations on one machine; its absolute value is meaningless.
A guarantee that a user never sees older data after having seen newer data.
Mutual TLS: both client and server present certificates, so each proves its identity to the other.
Replication where several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other.
An attention variant (Shazeer, 2019) in which all query heads share a single key/value head, shrinking the KV cache by the number of heads at some cost in quality.
A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where build tools live in early stages and only the finished output is copied into a small final image.
Uploading a large object as independently uploaded parts that are assembled at the end.
Carrying many independent streams over one connection at once, as HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do.
An SLO alert that fires only when the burn rate exceeds a threshold over both a long and a short window, with several thresholds for fast and slow burns (for example 14.4x over 1 hour and 5 minutes).
Multi-version concurrency control: keeping several versions of rows so each transaction reads a consistent snapshot.
Running one query for a list and then one more query per item to fetch related data.
Provisioning one spare instance beyond the N needed for peak load, so any single failure still leaves enough capacity.
Caching a 'not found' result, usually with a short TTL, so repeated lookups of a missing item don't reach the database.
A failure in which some nodes cannot exchange messages with others, though each may still be running. To the nodes it looks the same as a slow or paused peer.
A protocol that synchronises a machine's clock with time servers by estimating offset from request and reply timestamps. Its accuracy is limited by network delay and path asymmetry.
A widely used event-driven web server and reverse proxy.
Shorthand for availability percentages: three nines is 99.9% (about 8.76 hours of downtime a year), four nines 99.99% (about 52.6 minutes).
Organising tables so each fact is stored once, following normal forms such as 1NF to 3NF.
A DNS record naming the authoritative nameservers for a domain.
A framework (RFC 6749) for delegated authorization: an authorization server issues access tokens so an app can call an API on a user's behalf without seeing their password.
Storage that keeps whole objects (bytes plus metadata) under keys in flat buckets, accessed over HTTP.
A fixed collection of inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria, run against a prompt and model before shipping. Also called a golden set.
Online analytical processing: workloads that scan and aggregate large amounts of data.
Online transaction processing: workloads of many small, fast reads and writes of individual records.
Measuring LLM output quality on live production traffic with feedback signals, sampled automatic grading and distribution monitoring.
An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token, a signed JWT telling the client who logged in, plus discovery and a UserInfo endpoint.
A CNCF project providing vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, the OTLP protocol and a Collector for traces, metrics and logs.
Reading without locks and checking at write time that a version number hasn't changed.
The server that holds the authoritative copy of content, which a CDN or cache fetches from on a miss.
A regional cache layer between a CDN's edge locations and the origin, so each object is fetched from the origin about once instead of once per location.
Per-host health tracking in a load balancer or proxy that temporarily ejects an individual misbehaving replica, for example after consecutive 5xx responses, while the healthy ones keep serving.

A response that says the service itself is temporarily out of capacity, as distinct from a 429 that says the caller exceeded its quota. Anthropic's API documents HTTP 529 overloaded_error for this case.
Daniel Abadi's extension of CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.
What a B-tree does when an insert lands in a full page: it splits the page in two, each half-empty. Random keys cause frequent splits and a larger, less cache-friendly index.

vLLM's technique of storing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks mapped through a per-sequence block table, like virtual memory pages. It removes up-front reservation and lets sequences share prefix blocks.
A query whose SQL text is fixed with placeholders and parsed before values are supplied separately, so values can only ever be treated as data. Also called a prepared statement.
One independent, ordered, append-only log within a topic. Partitions are the unit of storage, consumer parallelism and ordering in Kafka.
A value attached to a message that is hashed to choose its partition, so all messages with the same key go to the same partition and stay in order.

Leslie Lamport's consensus algorithm, which decides a value in two majority phases (prepare/promise, then accept/accepted). Multi-Paxos, with a stable leader, underpins systems such as Google's Chubby and Spanner.
How many times higher the busiest period's traffic is than the average, typically 2–10×.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall; p99 latency is the time 99% of requests are at or under.
A GraphQL query registered ahead of time and sent by its hash or ID instead of its full text.
Data that identifies a person directly, such as a name or email, or in combination, such as birth date plus postcode. GDPR calls the broader category personal data.
Locking data before reading it for update, so other transactions wait.
A lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL that multiplexes many client connections onto fewer server connections.
A PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type, distance operators and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes, so embeddings can live beside the rows they describe.
Detecting personal data with patterns and named-entity recognition and removing or replacing it before it is sent, logged or stored. Detection is never perfect.
A disaster recovery tier where data is replicated live to a recovery region but application servers are switched off or at zero until a disaster.
The idle time while a pipeline fills and drains each step. For p stages and m micro-batches it is (p − 1)/(m + p − 1) of the total time.
Splitting a model by layers into stages on different GPUs and streaming micro-batches through them like an assembly line. Only boundary activations cross the network.
The go/no-go step of a saga. Steps before it must be compensatable; steps after it must be retriable until they succeed.
Proof Key for Code Exchange (RFC 7636): the client sends a hash of a random secret when requesting an authorization code and must present the secret to redeem it, so an intercepted code is useless.
The smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers that run together on one node and share an IP address and volumes. Pods are replaced, never repaired.
A CDN data centre located near users, from which cached content is served.
Restoring a physical base backup and replaying the archived change log up to a chosen moment, such as just before a bad statement ran.
A message that fails every time it is processed, however often it is retried, for example because its payload is malformed.
The component that evaluates access policy and returns allow or deny, such as Open Policy Agent. A separate enforcement point applies the answer.
A balancing method that picks two backends at random and sends the request to the less busy one; nearly as good as checking every backend.
The ordered nodes clockwise on a ring that store replicas of a key.
The maximum number of unacknowledged messages a broker will deliver to one consumer at a time; in RabbitMQ it is set with basic.qos.
The first phase of LLM inference, which processes all prompt tokens in one parallel forward pass and fills the KV cache. It is compute-bound and largely determines time to first token.

Running the prefill and decode phases of LLM inference on separate GPU pools and transferring the KV cache between them, so the phases stop interfering and each pool can be sized and configured separately.
Routing an LLM request to the replica most likely to already hold its prompt prefix in KV cache, balanced against replica load, instead of spreading requests blindly.
A time-limited URL, signed by a service's credentials, that lets a client perform one operation on one object.
The secret half of a key pair; it signs data or decrypts what the public key encrypted, and must never leave the owner.

Each reader randomly decides to refresh a cached value before it expires, with the chance rising as expiry approaches, so one reader usually refreshes it without locks. XFetch is the best-known algorithm.
An interval in which a running program makes no progress without knowing time passed, such as a stop-the-world garbage collection, VM migration or swapping.
The time a stream processor happens to observe an event, according to its own clock. It differs on every run and during backlogs.
A compression scheme that splits each vector into sub-vectors and stores each as a short centroid id, shrinking memory many times at the cost of approximate distances.
A read model built and kept up to date by consuming a stream of events, shaped for a specific query.
Reusing the computed KV state of an exactly repeated prompt prefix so later requests skip prefill for that part. The model still generates a fresh answer.
A workflow pattern where a fixed sequence of LLM calls each uses the previous call's output, with code checks between steps.
Untrusted text, typed by a user or hidden in fetched content, that tries to override an LLM application's instructions. Filters reduce it but cannot fully prevent it.
N-gram drafting that finds the most recent generated tokens elsewhere in the prompt and proposes the tokens that followed them. It works best when the output copies the input.
An automated run of the eval set on every prompt or model change that blocks the change if quality drops beyond set thresholds.
Google's binary, schema-based serialisation format where fields are identified by numeric tags.
Routing LLM calls to a second model provider, region or cloud when the primary is failing, usually behind a per-provider circuit breaker.
A function setting that keeps a chosen number of execution environments initialised in advance, so requests up to that level avoid cold starts. You pay for them whether or not they are used.
Capacity reserved for one customer, such as dedicated model replicas, so their traffic is isolated from other tenants. The reserved capacity is paid for whether or not it is used.
Replacing identifiers with stand-ins that can be linked back to the person using separately kept information. Under GDPR, pseudonymised data is still personal data.
The half of a key pair that can be shared; it encrypts data or verifies signatures made by the private key.
A messaging pattern where a publisher writes to a topic and every subscriber to that topic receives its own copy of each message.
A CDN that fetches content from the origin on the first request at each location and caches it according to its headers.
A CDN to which you upload content in advance, so it serves files without contacting an origin.
Queries (or requests) per second, the standard unit for load on a service.
Storing model weights or KV cache values with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, to save memory and bandwidth at some risk to output quality.
A transport protocol over UDP, with built-in TLS 1.3 and independent streams, that HTTP/3 runs on.
A minimum set of replicas that must take part for an operation to count, such as W replicas acknowledging a write or R replicas answering a read. A majority quorum is more than half of the nodes.
SGLang's prefix-caching mechanism: it keeps finished requests' KV cache in a radix tree keyed by tokens, reuses the longest matching prefix for new requests and evicts least-recently-used leaves.

A consensus algorithm (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) built around a single elected leader that replicates a log and commits entries once a majority stores them. Used by etcd, Consul, CockroachDB and Kafka's KRaft.
A numbered period in Raft that starts with an election and has at most one leader. Nodes reject messages from lower terms and step down when they see a higher one.
A component that caps how many requests a client can make in a period and rejects or delays the rest.
Role-based access control: permissions are granted to roles and users are assigned roles, so access follows job function.
A Redis point-in-time dump of the whole dataset to a compact file, written by a forked child process.
Resilient distributed dataset: Spark's immutable, partitioned collection that records its lineage so lost partitions can be recomputed rather than replicated.
Fixing stale replicas during a read by writing the newest version seen back to the replicas that returned older ones.
A caching strategy where the application reads only from the cache and the cache itself loads missing entries from the database.
A guarantee that a user always sees their own earlier writes.
How many reads a system serves for each write; it decides whether to optimise for reads (caches, replicas) or writes.
A periodic check that decides whether a pod should receive traffic. On failure the pod is removed from Service endpoints but keeps running.
Reassigning a consumer group's partitions when members join, leave or are presumed dead, which pauses some consumption and can cause redelivery.
The fraction of the true top k nearest neighbours (found by brute force) that a search actually returned in its top k. It measures how approximate an ANN index is.
A way to merge ranked lists by giving each item the sum of 1 / (k + rank) across lists, usually with k = 60. It uses ranks only, so incompatible score scales do not matter.
The pattern every Kubernetes controller follows: repeatedly compare the desired state with the observed state and take a step to close the gap.
The maximum amount of data, measured in time, that a system can afford to lose in a disaster.
The maximum acceptable time from the start of a disaster until the service is working again.
The DNS server (often your ISP's, or 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1) that chases a lookup through root, TLD and authoritative servers and caches the answer.
Tom Wilkie's checklist for request-driven services: measure Rate, Errors and Duration for every service.
A Redis append-only log of entries with time-based IDs, read by consumer groups that acknowledge entries with XACK.
A distributed lock algorithm by Redis's author that acquires the same key on a majority of independent Redis nodes within the lock's TTL. Its safety under clock and timing faults is debated.
Moving messages from a dead-letter queue back to their source queue to be processed again, usually after the underlying bug is fixed.
Running more instances of a component than the load needs, so the service survives losing some. It only works with spare capacity, failure detection and a way to shift work.
A long-lived credential sent only to the authorization server to obtain new access tokens. Because it is checked server-side, it can be revoked.
The rule that accepts a draft token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)) and, on rejection, samples from norm(max(0, p − q)). It makes the output follow the target distribution p exactly.
A database that stores data in tables with a fixed schema, linked by keys and queried with SQL.
A guarantee that every byte arrives, in order, by retransmitting anything not acknowledged.
Re-asking the model with its invalid output and the exact validation error so it can return a corrected version, limited to one or two attempts.
A copy of a database that receives changes from a leader; read replicas serve read queries.
A design where every node starts in the same state and applies the same commands in the same order, so all nodes end in the same state. Consensus is used to agree on the command order.
The number of replicas (N) that store each piece of data.
The delay between a write on the leader and that write appearing on a follower.
Merging concurrent requests for the same key so only one fetch runs and the others share its result. Also called request collapsing.
A priority label attached to each request, such as CRITICAL or SHEDDABLE, that tells overloaded servers which requests to reject first.
The pattern where a client sends one request and waits for one response from the server.
A per-function setting that sets aside part of the account's concurrency pool for that function and caps it at that amount. Setting it to zero stops the function.
Moving data to a new shard layout, usually to add capacity, while the system stays online.
A proxy reading the whole backend response quickly, freeing the backend, then feeding it to a slow client itself.
An architectural style for web APIs: resources with URIs, acted on with standard HTTP methods, exchanging representations such as JSON.
An architecture that retrieves relevant passages from your own documents at question time and places them in the model's prompt so it can answer from them and cite them.
The multiplication of load when several layers each retry: k attempts at each of L layers send up to k^L calls to the bottom service.
A cap on retries as a fraction of normal requests (for example 10%), so worst-case load stays near 1.1 times normal however many calls fail.
A surge of synchronised or multiplied retries that overloads a service just as it is trying to recover, often prolonging the outage.
A server in front of your backends that receives client requests on their behalf and forwards them.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimise the model against that reward (for example with PPO) while limiting drift from the starting model.
Replacing instances of the old version with the new one in batches, so some capacity always serves traffic and two versions run side by side during the rollout.

A performance model (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009) in which attainable throughput is the lower of peak FLOP/s and memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity. The ridge point, peak FLOP/s ÷ bandwidth, separates memory-bound from compute-bound work.
The top of the DNS hierarchy; it points resolvers to the right top-level-domain servers.
A balancing method that sends each new request to the next server in a fixed rotation.
A string attached to a RabbitMQ message when it is published, such as order.eu.created, which exchanges match against bindings.
Calling a function that runs on another machine as if it were a local function call.
A short document linked from an alert that explains what the alert means for users and the steps to confirm, mitigate and escalate it. Also called a playbook.
An HTTP method that should not change server state, such as GET or HEAD.
A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action, that either all complete or have the completed ones undone. It gives up isolation in exchange for avoiding distributed locks.
Running a saga without a central coordinator: each service reacts to other services' events and publishes its own, so the flow emerges from the subscriptions.
Running a saga from a central orchestrator that tells each service which step to perform and durably records progress, for example with Temporal or AWS Step Functions.
An empirical power-law relationship between a model's loss and its parameter count, training tokens and compute, used to predict results and plan budgets before training.
A high-capacity network location run by a DDoS mitigation provider that receives a victim's traffic, filters out attack traffic and forwards the clean remainder.
Drafting with a cheaper version of the target model itself, for example its first layers with an early exit, then verifying with the full model.
A response cache that returns a stored answer when a new query's embedding is similar enough to an earlier query's, skipping the model call entirely.
A dummy node at the start or end of a linked list that is never removed, so insert and unlink code never has to handle empty-list edge cases.
A counter on every TCP segment that marks its position in the byte stream, so the receiver can reorder and detect gaps.
A consistency model (Lamport, 1979) in which all operations appear in one total order that respects each client's own order, but not necessarily real time.
A program that waits for requests and answers them. One process can be a server to some callers and a client of others.
A browser standard where the server streams text events over one long-lived HTTP response, with automatic reconnect.
An attack that makes a server send requests to destinations the attacker chooses, reaching internal services or cloud metadata endpoints from inside the trust boundary.
A stable name and virtual IP for the ready pods that match a label selector, so clients do not depend on individual pod IPs.
A contract with customers that states consequences, usually service credits, if a service level is missed. It is normally set looser than the internal SLO.
A carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of a service, best written as good events divided by valid events, such as the fraction of requests that succeed.
A target value for an SLI over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over a rolling 28 days.
A layer of sidecar proxies plus a control plane that handles service-to-service routing, retries, mTLS and telemetry.
Data that ties a series of requests to one user, such as login status or a cart, usually found by a session id in a cookie.
Four per-client guarantees defined for the Bayou system: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads.
A window that groups one key's events separated by less than an inactivity gap; it has no fixed length and can merge when a late event bridges two sessions.
A copy of real production requests sent to a new version of a service whose responses are recorded and compared but never returned to users.
The column or value that decides which shard a row is stored on.
Splitting one dataset's rows across several databases by a key, so each database holds a slice.
The client asks the server for updates on a fixed timer; the server answers at once, usually with nothing.
The step between map and reduce that partitions intermediate data by key, moves it across the network from every mapper to every reducer, and sorts it so equal keys are together.
A proxy process deployed next to each service instance that handles its network traffic.
Hardware computing or storing wrong values without raising any error. In training it may show up only as unexplained loss or gradient anomalies.
The minimum similarity score at which a vector match is accepted, for example as a semantic cache hit. Lowering it raises both hits and false hits.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down because nothing else can take over (SPOF).

A fixed-size time window that advances by a smaller slide, so windows overlap and each event belongs to size ÷ slide windows. Flink calls these sliding windows; Kafka Streams calls them hopping windows.
The amount of unacknowledged data a sender may have in flight; it slides forward as ACKs arrive.
A quorum that may count acknowledgements from stand-in nodes outside a key's home replicas when those are unreachable, trading the read-write overlap guarantee for write availability.
The share of calls in a breaker's window that took longer than a set duration. A high slow-call rate can trip a breaker before calls start failing outright.
A 64-bit ID packing a millisecond timestamp, a machine ID and a per-millisecond sequence, introduced by Twitter. Any generator can mint roughly time-ordered IDs locally.
A Redis data type holding unique members each with a numeric score, kept ordered by score, with O(log N) updates and rank lookups.
The authoritative store for a piece of data, usually a database. Caches and replicas hold copies that may lag behind it.
One named, timed operation in a trace, such as an HTTP handler or a database query, with its own ID, a parent ID, attributes and status.
Speeding up generation by letting a cheap drafter propose several tokens that the large target model verifies in one forward pass. With the exact acceptance rule the output distribution is unchanged.
A CNCF standard for workload identity: each workload gets a URI identity (spiffe://trust-domain/path) proven by a short-lived X.509 or JWT credential called an SVID.
A failure where two nodes both act as leader and accept conflicting writes.
An attack in which untrusted input pasted into SQL text is parsed as part of the query, changing what it does. Prevented by parameterised queries.
Secure Sockets Layer, TLS's deprecated predecessor; the name survives in everyday speech.
A read that returns a value older than the latest committed write in the source of truth.
A Cache-Control extension (RFC 5861) that lets a cache keep serving a stale copy for a set time after it expires while it fetches a fresh copy in the background.
A check that holds off liveness and readiness probes until a slow-starting container has finished starting, and restarts it if it never does.
A lock on infrastructure state that stops two applies running at once and overwriting each other's changes.
A server that keeps data between requests in its own memory or disk, so some requests must reach that specific server.
A server that keeps no request-to-request data in its own memory or disk, so any copy can handle any request.
A Kafka consumer setting (group.instance.id) that lets a consumer restarting quickly reclaim its partitions without triggering a rebalance.
A design in which a system keeps working through a dependency failure without having to make any changes in response, for example by pre-provisioning capacity. The term is used by AWS.
A three-digit number in an HTTP response stating the result, grouped 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
A measurable claim that a business-level metric will stay within stated bounds while a specific fault is injected; the experiment tries to disprove it.
A hard cap, enforced by the orchestrator, on how many loop iterations an agent run may take before it is stopped.
A long-lived connection that stays bound to one server for its whole life, so it cannot be moved without reconnecting.
Load balancer routing that sends each user back to the same server, usually because their session lives in that server's memory.
An automatic rule that halts a chaos experiment and removes the fault when a guard metric crosses a threshold.
A task that runs much slower than its peers and so delays the whole job; MapReduce counters slow machines with backup tasks (speculative execution).
Replacing an old system gradually by routing one capability at a time to new code until the old code can be deleted.
The longest a client will wait between chunks of a streamed response before treating the stream as stalled.
Computing continuously over an unbounded sequence of events as they arrive, keeping state between events instead of waiting for a complete input.
Recovering a streamed generation after a replica fails by resubmitting the prompt plus the tokens already sent to a healthy replica and continuing from there.
Writing each log event as named fields, usually one JSON object per line, so logs can be queried by field instead of parsed with regexes.
Model output in a defined machine-readable format, such as JSON matching a schema, so code can consume it. It still needs validation before use.
The small DNS client in your operating system that forwards lookups to a recursive resolver.
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on curated examples of desired responses, usually the first post-training stage.
A tag attached to cached responses so that one purge request can invalidate every object with that tag. Fastly calls it Surrogate-Key; Cloudflare calls it Cache-Tag.
Paging on what users experience, such as failed or slow requests, rather than on internal causes such as high CPU, which are used for diagnosis instead.
The 'synchronise' flag on the first TCP packet, which asks to open a connection and carries the starting sequence number.
A TCP defence against SYN floods in which the server encodes connection details in its initial sequence number and stores no state until a valid ACK returns.
The latency of the slowest requests, usually p99 and above.
Buffering all spans and deciding after a trace completes whether to keep it, so slow and failed traces can always be kept.
Transmission Control Protocol: a connection-based transport that delivers a reliable, ordered byte stream between two hosts.
A number that divides the logits before the softmax. Below 1 it sharpens the distribution toward the top token; above 1 it flattens it.

Splitting each layer's weight matrices across GPUs so they compute the same tokens together, as in Megatron-LM's column/row split. It needs activation-sized all-reduces in every layer, so it is kept inside a node's fast interconnect.
Terraform's preview of the creates, updates and destroys needed to make real infrastructure match the code, shown before anything changes.
A plugin that translates Terraform resources into API calls for one platform, such as AWS, Cloudflare or GitHub.
The file mapping each resource address in Terraform code to the real object's ID and last-seen attributes; it can contain secrets.
The guideline to write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end tests, because cost and flakiness rise with scope.
A relevance score that weights how often a term appears in a document by how rare the term is overall.
The SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection; it costs one round trip before data can flow.
How many operations complete per unit of time, such as requests per second.
A dedicated service whose only job is to hand out unique, increasing integer IDs to other servers, often in blocks so callers rarely need a round trip.
The average gap between successive streamed output tokens, also called inter-token latency. Per-user tokens per second is its inverse.
The time from sending an LLM request to receiving its first output token, covering queueing, prefill and the first decode step.
A database optimised for timestamped data that is mostly appended and queried by time range.
A client-side limit on how long to wait for the first streamed token of an LLM response. It catches an overloaded or stuck provider much sooner than a total timeout.
The longest a caller will wait for an operation before giving up and treating it as failed. It says nothing about whether the operation actually happened.
