The user's total allowed wait treated as one budget that every hop in a call chain spends from, instead of independent per-hop timeouts.
A server for a top-level domain such as .com that points to each domain's authoritative nameservers.
Transport Layer Security: the protocol that encrypts and authenticates traffic, the 'S' in HTTPS.
The opening exchange where client and server agree on algorithms, verify the certificate and derive shared session keys.
Letting a proxy do TLS encryption and decryption so backend servers do not have to.
Decrypting TLS at a proxy or load balancer, which then forwards plain or re-encrypted traffic to backends.
A subword piece of text from a model's fixed tokenizer vocabulary, the unit in which LLM context limits, throughput and prices are measured. English averages roughly four characters per token.
A rate-limiting algorithm with a bucket of up to B tokens refilled at R per second; each request spends a token.
An explicit limit on tokens at some scope, such as per call, per conversation, per user per day or per feature, used to control LLM cost and latency.
Splitting text into individual terms (tokens) for indexing or searching.
Replacing a sensitive value such as a card number with a random token, while the real value is kept only in a guarded token vault. The token has no mathematical link to the value.
A provider rate limit on the number of tokens an account or project may process per minute. For LLM workloads it usually binds before the requests-per-minute limit.
A marker written in place of deleted data that records the deletion, so that replicas which missed the delete do not bring the data back. Tombstones are purged after a grace period.
A model returning a structured request to run a named tool with JSON arguments, which the application executes and returns the result of. Also called function calling.
Keeping only the k most likely tokens, renormalising their probabilities and sampling among them.

Keeping the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities sum to at least p, then sampling among them, so the set shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is not (Holtzman et al., 2020).
A saved snapshot of everything needed to resume training exactly: weights, optimiser state, learning-rate schedule position, random-number states and the data loader position.
A group of reads and writes that the database treats as one unit.
The node that runs two-phase commit: it sends PREPARE, collects votes, durably logs the commit or abort decision and delivers it to participants.
A pattern that writes an event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change, then publishes it to the broker with a separate relay or CDC process.
Verifying several candidate continuations in one forward pass by arranging them as a tree and masking attention so each candidate sees only its own branch.
A tree that stores strings by their characters, so strings sharing a prefix share a path.
In the Dataflow Model, the rule that decides when a window emits a result: early speculative results, an on-time result at the watermark, and late updates.
The condition that moves a circuit breaker from closed to open, such as a failure rate above 50% over the window or a number of consecutive failures.

Google Spanner's clock API, which returns a time interval guaranteed to contain the true time, using GPS and atomic clocks. Spanner waits out the uncertainty to give globally consistent commit timestamps.
A branching model where everyone merges small changes into one main branch at least daily, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags instead of long-lived branches.
Time to live: how many seconds a DNS answer may be cached before it must be looked up again.
Adding a random amount to each key's time to live so keys written together don't all expire at the same moment.
A fixed-size, non-overlapping time window such as each whole minute; every event belongs to exactly one window.
A set of guidelines for building cloud services, written at Heroku; factor VI says app processes should be stateless and share nothing.
A protocol that commits a transaction across several databases atomically: a coordinator collects prepare votes, logs a decision and tells every participant to commit or abort.
A DNS record holding free text, used for domain verification and email security such as SPF.
Suggesting completions of a query as the user types.
User Datagram Protocol: a connectionless transport that sends independent packets with no delivery, ordering or retransmission guarantees.
Brendan Gregg's checklist for every resource: check Utilization, Saturation (work waiting) and Errors.
The fraction of time a resource is busy. Queueing delay grows sharply as it approaches 100%.

A 128-bit universally unique identifier that any machine can generate without coordination. A few bits mark its version, which decides how the rest are filled (random in v4, timestamp plus random in v7).

A UUID version defined in RFC 9562 whose first 48 bits are a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, followed by random bits. It sorts by creation time, which keeps B-tree inserts at the right edge of the index.
A separate JavaScript heap and execution context inside one shared V8 engine process. Edge platforms such as Cloudflare Workers use isolates so code starts far faster than a container.
An HTTP response header listing which request headers change the response, so caches store a separate copy for each value.
An array of counters, one per process, attached to events. Comparing two vectors entry by entry shows whether one event happened before the other or whether they were concurrent.
A cache key that includes a version number, so a write bumps the version and readers move to a new key while old entries age out.
Scaling up: giving one machine more CPU, memory, disk or network capacity.
An IP address not tied to one machine, which can move to a standby when the active node fails.
One of many positions a physical node takes on a consistent hashing ring, used to even out load.
In Amazon SQS, how long a received message is hidden from other consumers; if it isn't deleted before the timeout ends, it becomes visible and is delivered again.
A disaster recovery tier where a scaled-down but fully working copy of the stack runs in a recovery region, ready to take traffic and scale up.
A stream processor's running estimate that event time has reached T, meaning no more events older than T are expected. Event-time windows fire when the watermark passes their end.
A filter in front of a web application that inspects HTTP requests and blocks ones matching attack patterns or rules. It is a safety net, not a replacement for secure code.
A protocol, started by an HTTP upgrade, that keeps one TCP connection open for two-way messages in small frames.
Round robin where bigger servers get proportionally more turns.
A database that groups rows by partition key across nodes and sorts them by clustering key within each partition.
The subset of data actively used over a period of time. A cache that holds the working set gets a high hit ratio even if the full dataset is much larger.
A credential a running service receives from its platform because of what and where it is, instead of a static secret in its configuration. It is usually short-lived and rotated automatically.
The ratio of bytes written to storage to bytes the application asked to write.
An anomaly where two transactions read the same data, write different rows, and together violate a rule.
A caching strategy where writes go only to the database and the cache is filled later, only if the data is read.
A caching strategy where writes are acknowledged once the cache has them and flushed to the database asynchronously, risking loss of unflushed writes.
A caching strategy where each write updates the cache and the database synchronously, and is acknowledged only when both succeed.

The Zero Redundancy Optimizer (Rajbhandari et al., 2020): data parallelism that shards optimiser state (stage 1), gradients (stage 2) and weights (stage 3) across ranks instead of replicating them. PyTorch FSDP implements the same idea.

A string that encodes a latitude/longitude cell by interleaving the bits of both coordinates and writing them in base 32; nearby points usually share a prefix, so a prefix scan finds candidates near a location (cells on either side of a boundary can share none, so searches also check neighbouring cells).

Uber's open-source hierarchical geospatial index that tiles the Earth in hexagons at 16 resolutions; every neighbour of a hexagon is the same distance away, which makes radius searches and area aggregates (such as supply and demand per cell) more even than square grids.

An accounting record where every movement of money is written as at least two entries, a debit and a credit, that sum to zero; balances are derived from the entries, so money can never appear or vanish without an entry showing where it came from.

A queue in front of a site that admits visitors at the rate the backend can serve and holds the rest on a cheap, cacheable waiting page, turning a sudden crowd into a steady flow instead of an overload.

A schedule written as five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week), such as 0 2 * * * for 02:00 every day; schedulers turn it into the next fire times, and time zones and daylight-saving changes are the usual sources of bugs.

A circular array of buckets, one per time tick, where a timer is dropped into the bucket for its expiry and a pointer advances one bucket per tick; adding and expiring timers is O(1), which is why schedulers and Kafka use it for millions of timers (Varghese and Lauck, 1987).

A tree that splits a 2-D area into four quadrants and keeps splitting any quadrant holding too many points, so dense cities get small cells and empty areas big ones; used to find nearby points without scanning everything.
Decoding a media file and re-encoding it into other formats, resolutions or bitrates, for example turning one uploaded video into a set of renditions for different screens and networks.
The set of renditions a video is encoded into, each a resolution and bitrate pair (such as 1080p at 5 Mb/s down to 240p at 300 kb/s), that an adaptive player switches between.

Delivering video as short segments at several bitrates and letting the player pick the next segment's bitrate from measured bandwidth and buffer level, so playback continues at lower quality instead of stalling.

HTTP Live Streaming (RFC 8216): a playlist of short media segments fetched over plain HTTP, with a master playlist listing the available bitrates; because it is just files over HTTP, CDNs cache it like any other content.
Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (ISO/IEC 23009-1): the standards-body counterpart of HLS, describing segments and bitrates in an XML manifest (MPD).
Common Media Application Format (ISO/IEC 23000-19): a fragmented-MP4 segment format that both HLS and DASH can reference, so one set of encoded segments serves both protocols and halves CDN storage.
A property the system must have rather than a feature it offers, stated as a measurable target: latency (e.g. under 50 ms at p99), availability, consistency, durability, throughput or cost.
In an interview, announcing where you are and what you will do next ('That's requirements; next, two minutes of estimation'), so the interviewer can follow or redirect you cheaply.
Giving each step of a task a fixed time budget and moving on when it runs out, even if the step feels unfinished; in a design interview, the 5/5/5/5/10/10/5 split for 45 minutes.

A piece of evidence an interviewer notes about how a candidate would work at a given level, such as deriving peak load unprompted or raising failure modes without a hint. Interviewers usually form an overall picture from many signals rather than adding up points.

Deciding what happens next in a design interview and saying why (an agenda, assumptions, which deep dive to take), then asking for a quick confirmation, while still following the interviewer when they steer.

A data store whose main index finds the stored vectors closest to a query vector, usually with an approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW. Used for semantic search, recommendations and RAG retrieval; the same capability is also offered as an extension or feature of general-purpose databases and search engines.

Splitting one hot key into several sub-keys, for example by appending hash(user_id) mod N, so its writes spread over several partitions. Reading a total then means combining the sub-keys, usually through an asynchronously maintained counter.
Sending one request to many shards in parallel and merging their answers. Latency is set by the slowest shard, so rare per-shard slowness becomes common at high fan-out.
When an item at the front of a FIFO queue or connection holds up everything behind it, for example urgent messages stuck behind a large bulk backlog in the same partition.
Periodically comparing your records with an external party's records, such as a payment provider's settlement report, matching them by a shared reference and resolving every mismatch.

A study method that schedules each review just as you are likely to forget, with intervals that grow after each successful recall and reset after a failure. The flashcards here use the classic SM-2 algorithm (1 day, 6 days, then the interval times an ease factor).

Reducing study volume in the final days before an interview while keeping short, focused retrieval practice, so you arrive rested rather than tired. Borrowed from endurance sport, where training volume is cut before a race.

Something a user or caller must be able to do with the system, written as a verb phrase: 'create a short link', 'hold up to 4 seats for 10 minutes'. Functional requirements drive the API and data model.

A rule that must hold in every state of the system, such as 'a seat is never sold twice' or 'a buyer is charged exactly once'. Violating it even once is a correctness failure, so it usually needs a dedicated mechanism (conditional write, lock, idempotency key).

A short running list kept on the whiteboard during a design interview: each decision that had a real alternative, the alternative, and the reason it lost. It anchors answers to pushback and becomes the trade-off summary at wrap-up.

The condition stated alongside a design decision under which the rejected alternative would win, for example "if writes grew a thousandfold, switch to counter blocks." It shows the decision is tied to current numbers rather than taste.
A timed rehearsal of a real interview, alone against a clock or with a partner playing the interviewer, followed by scoring against a rubric and feedback.
A list of criteria, each with a written description of what earns 0, 1 or 2 points, used to score a design attempt by evidence rather than impression.
